messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Forty-four-year-old Dat Nguyen was walking home from his night shift at the county hospital when the mugging occurred. The violence was sudden, leaving a heavy pressure across his ribs and a sharp, grinding ache in his left shoulder where the man’s elbow had driven into him. He remembered the attacker’s face not as a continuous scene but as a series of sharp, static frames: the glint of the knife, the wide eyes, the tension in the jaw. When the memory returns, he feels physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event, the old pressure and ache surfacing without warning. His memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images, and remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in his mind. Over the next several weeks, those photographs began to appear alongside his daily routine. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that there is something about him that made the event happen, and that he carries a quiet hopelessness alongside his daily tasks. By the third month, his environment and his habits had aligned into a steady pattern of observation. At the nurse’s station, he never sat in the open aisles. He always chooses where to sit based on how safe or protected he feels, tucking his chair against the wall or near the corner partition so he could brace against passing equipment. He kept the hallway mirrors within his line of sight, keep checking mirrors to ensure his own reflection was steady and unthreatened. His mind never rested; he kept mind occupied all the time, mentally tallying floor tiles, reciting medication dosages, and tracking the rhythmic beeping of the cardiac monitor. He constantly scans environment for signs of threat, his eyes moving toward doorways, elevators, and the central supply carts. When he walks to his car after a shift, he frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, his shoulders held tight, his steps measured. These habits have accumulated quietly over months. His wife has noticed how he lingers in the living room chair angled toward the street, and at work he avoids the sudden movement of rolling carts, holding his body ready. He held his sleep problems alongside his vigilance, lying in bed for hours, trouble falling or staying asleep because the quiet room felt dangerously exposed. He did not attribute his waking hours to his nights, nor his scanning to his seating; these states simply coexisted in his life, each present and distinct. What finally brought Dat to seek help was the way the fear had settled into his routine and his bed. He lay awake for hours, the photographs of the mugging surfacing without warning, pressing against his ribs and shoulder, and he sat up, certain that the danger remained. He was most afraid of losing the careful balance he had built, of the slow accumulation of waiting that seemed to fill his days. What he hoped for was not to forget the event, but to understand why it had happened to him, and to find a way to move through the hospital, his car, and his home without bracing for impact.
